Print the curator's message(s) at a UTC timestamp or its prefix, verbatim.

    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53          # every message of his in that minute
    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53:07.5     # a finer prefix
    python3 -I show.py --list 2026-10-12         # one line per message (timestamp, source, length, start)
    python3 -I show.py --count                   # how many messages the three sources give

A prefix may use a space instead of the T and may end in Z. All times are UTC.

His messages come from three places, and the header of each printed message says which:
  main  the main-session lines of the transcripts in /root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/
        and /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/projects/-home-user-fortress/ (the .parts
        folders included): `user` lines that are not isMeta, not sidechain, with text content
        that does not start with '<' and is not a compaction summary; deduplicated by uuid,
        because a resumed transcript replays earlier lines.
  s1    the same lines of the first coordinating session (bdff267d), read with `git show` from
        the `transcripts` branch (origin/transcripts) of this repository, 2026-08-18 to 2026-09-17.
        Skipped, with a note on stderr, if that branch is not in the clone.
  queued  a message he queued while an agent was busy that no `user` line holds as its text
        (the queue-operation `enqueue` lines and the queued_command attachments); its time is the
        time he sent it.
Nothing is filtered by author or by kind: a scheduled check-in or a pasted report that arrived as a
`user` line is printed too, so a reader decides what is his.

=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== hischeck.py
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per

You didn't contradict anything. The checker as it landed in batch N contradicts your decision, and option 1 fixes the checker.

The example: `a: V = k(NOf(1))`, with two declarations of `k`.
- `k[\T extends N\](x: T): T` is generic. It fits the argument as it is, and returns an `N`.
- `k(x: V): V` is plain. It fits only if `NOf(1)` is first converted to `V`.
- The result must go into `a: V`, and an `N` can be converted to `V`.

Your decision 1 says a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. So the generic `k` should run, and its `N` result gets converted to `V` at the assignment. Walk does exactly that.

What the landed checker does:
1. Its first attempt matches without any conversion, but it also demands that the result already be a `V`. The generic's result is an `N`, so the generic is ruled out.
2. Its second attempt allows conversions and finds `k(V)`, by converting the argument.

So the compiled program runs `k(V)` and walk runs the generic. The two paths disagree, and the compiled one goes against your rule.

Option 1 reorders the first attempt: match without conversion and without demanding the result type, keep the winner if its result can be converted to `V`, and only then try conversions. That's your rule as written. It's one checker rung, in batch 8.

That's all there is to it. The audit's section 6, item 4 says the same in four lines.

- How far? Not far, and not in the direction of a redesign. The errors are in the record and in one landed rung, not in the language. The risk that remains is of omission: the three least designed pieces, the switch-over, the sized model and the unboxed store, are the ones the goal depends on, and every batch since 2026-09-26 has been spent before them.

## 6. For Pavol

In the order needed. Each is one question, its context, numbered options with what each touches and costs, and a recommendation last.

### 1. Does `floor` on a float return a float or an unbounded integer? (row 330; reverse or restate, before it is built)

- The team's word on floats, in the 2008 release and the interpreter's api, is consistent: `floor` and `ceiling` return the float, the brackets and `truncate` an integer (`ZZ64`). Only the component body and the prelude's comment are inconsistent, and only for the brackets, `truncate` and `round`.
- Your reason of 2026-09-21 rested on ℤ sitting under ℝ64; under route A it does not, so an integer result rejoins float arithmetic only through a written `asFloat`.
- Nothing is built. Options:
  1. The named functions keep the float, as every text of the team's and every peer has it; the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return ℤ, as the rational chapter's rule and your no-overflow reasoning have it, tidying the team's three spellings to one. Touches: the `RR64` api and body (five lines), the ledger row, POSITIONS:47, and later a specification sentence for the float types. Costs one library rung after the switch-over, as planned.
  2. Keep the decision as it stands, all ℤ, with the reason restated on coercion: every float program that floors and continues in float arithmetic writes `asFloat`. Touches the same lines plus every such caller. Costs the same rung and a notation tax on users.
  3. The 2008 listing whole: `floor` float, brackets and `truncate` `ZZ64`, `round` `ZZ64`. Touches the same lines. Costs the silent saturation past 2^63 that both paths have today.
- Recommendation: 1.

### 2. What does the compiled path do with a call whose result type is `Bottom`? (row 447, item 18; before phase 4)

- Batch 7 wrote `extends Object` on `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and the nullary comprehension, as decided; the solver then binds a result-only parameter to `Bottom`, the type with no values. For the natives that is harmless. For `fail` it is not: every value-position `fail("...")` in the library now compiles and fails JVM verification at load, where the checker refused it before.
- The 2012 Types chapter says `Bottom` is uninhabited and cannot be written; the specification already gives a `throw` expression that type.
- Options:
  1. The code generator treats a call typed `Bottom` as it treats a `throw`: the call is made and the code after it is unreachable, so no value is returned where a `ZZ32` is expected. Touches `CodeGen`; one rung with row 447's two probes as its tests; the written bounds stay.
  2. Refuse a value-position call whose result-only parameter nothing fixes, as answer 12 does for sizes. Touches the checker and every library `fail` site, each of which then writes its static argument. Costs a library sweep and brings back the errors rung B cleared at `fail`.
  3. Take the prelude's `fail(s: String): Zilch`, a declared bottom type. Outside the specification; walk cannot evaluate it.
- Recommendation: 1, as a prerequisite of phase 4, not a phase-5 item.

### 3. Is the implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter `Any`, as the library and walk take it, or `Object`, as the draft says? (Q1; before batch 7b's rung S)

- The draft says `Object` (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`). The library declares its element types unbounded and instantiates them at tuples, which `Object` excludes; walk and the gate's count read `Any`; the compile path's desugarer writes `Object` (row 412). The 2012 Types chapter has `Any` as the top. Batch 7 took `Any` as a default inside decision 2 and listed it; the overloading judgement had called it your decision.
- Options:
  1. `Any`, stated in the text with a callout, the compile path's `Object` setting named as the divergence until the switch-over collapses it. Touches one sentence and the naked-`Any` overloading rule, which rung S must then state as the checker reads it. Costs nothing new.
  2. `Object`, the draft's word. Touches the library: 163 refusals, mostly tuple index types, and the arrays' element types. Costs a library sweep against the library's own practice.
- Recommendation: 1, said in so many words.

### 4. In which order does the checker try a call's candidates? (row 508, item 34; phase 3)

- Rung I tries subtyping under the expected type first, so a declaration reached only by coercion whose result fits can win over a generic that fits the arguments as they are. That contradicts your decision 1 of 2026-09-28 and the coercion chapter's Σ. It is gated as an expected failure.
- Options:
  1. Try subtyping without the context first and keep it when its winner's result converts to the expected type, then coercion with the context. Touches `Functionals.scala`'s attempt order; one checker rung with `XXXInferContextKeepsFit` promoted. Costs one rung in batch 8.
  2. Leave it gated, with a workaround (write the static argument).
- Recommendation: 1.

### 5. Is the switch-over sized and its natives' shape probed now, in parallel with phase 3? (phase 4)

(* A generic declaration that fits the call without coercion is chosen over one reached by coercion whose result fits the expected type; ledger row 508. *)
component InferContextKeepsFit
export Executable

trait N
  getter n(): ZZ32
end
object NOf(k: ZZ32) extends N
  getter n(): ZZ32 = k
end
trait V excludes { N }
  coerce(x: N) = VOf(x.n)
  getter n(): ZZ32
end
object VOf(k: ZZ32) extends V
  getter n(): ZZ32 = k
end

k[\T extends N\](x: T): T = x
k(x: V): V = VOf(99)

run(): () = do
    a: V = k(NOf(1))
    assert(a.n, 1, "a: V = k(NOf(1)) runs the generic k, which fits NOf(1) without coercion, and converts its result to V, so a.n is 1 and not the 99 of k(V); Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex, section \"Coercion Resolution\"; Specification/basic/inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\"")
    println("PASS")
end

end
tests=InferContextKeepsFit
run
run_out_contains=PASS

REPORT.md
SKEPTIC.md
decision-record.md

**D1. Where the bound is computed: a call-only mode of the solver (`Formula.solveToBounds`), not a change of the shared `solve` or of `killIvars`.** Candidates: (a) change `slv` for every caller; (b) change `STypesUtil.killIvars` to bind `Any`; (c) post-process the solution in `inferStaticParamsHelper`; (d) a mode of `slv` that the call inference selects. (a) and (b) also reach `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.subUA` and `subEDsolution` (`scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala`, the two `inferStaticParamsHelper` calls), which ask whether *some* instance of a generic arrow makes one arrow a subtype of another: an existence question that the overloading checker asks (rung O's area), where `Bottom` is a legitimate witness and the paper's instance rule does not apply; (b) also changes the ancestor heuristic's trial maps (`Formula.scala`, the `proposedMap` line). (c) cannot see the meet with the expected type, which lives in the reduced formula's upper bounds. (d) changes only what a call instantiates. Taken: (d). `inferStaticParamsHelper` gains `toBounds` (default false); `inferStaticParams` (the subtyping attempt, and the coercion oracle's inference of a generic coercion's own parameters), `inferLiftedStaticParams` (a method's trait parameters, from its receiver) and the coercion attempt (`checkApplicableWithCoercion`) pass true; `TypeSchemaAnalyzer` and `addParamTypes` keep `solve`.

**D2. What `solveToBounds` does.** A type inference variable whose lower bounds are all `BottomType` or mention inference variables takes `ta.meet` of its upper bounds free of inference variables (its declared bound, instantiated, and what the expected type's constraint put there); if that meet is `BottomType` (the bound and the expected type exclude each other) the formula has no solution, never a `Bottom` binding; a variable the formula leaves unconstrained (the trivially true formula, a variable reduced away, a class of the unifier with no named member) takes `Any` (`STypesUtil.topIvars`), since only a top bound reduces away. A variable with a named lower bound is solved as before (the join, then the ancestor heuristic), which is the lone-parameter and argument-fixed case the chapter already describes. Alternatives refused: keeping `Bottom` as a lower bound that fixes the parameter at `Bottom` (an argument typed `Bottom`, a `throw`, says nothing about the instance; the decision says never `Bottom`); falling back to `Bottom` where the meet is empty (the batch record's stop: "A parameter nothing fixes bound to anything but its bounds under the expected type").

**D3. The promotion of a lone parameter's union offers "its upper bounds" (`None`) beside the named candidates, rather than adding the bound `Object` or `Any` to the named list.** `checkApplicableWithCoercion`'s `named` list excluded `Object` and `Any` as bounds; adding them would give `Object` where the expected type requires something narrower (`x: Number = pick0(w, r)` under `T` bounded by `Object` needs `Number`, the meet). The `None` choice leaves the parameter to the solver, which under D2 gives exactly the intersection of the upper bounds, context included. The narrowest of the candidates found still wins, so a written trait bound (`InferLoneBound`) and answer 8's number case are unchanged.

**D4. The order: subtyping without the context, then subtyping with it, then coercion with it, then coercion without it.** The decision's words are "subtyping without the expected type first and keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, then tries coercion with the context". Candidates: (a) drop the attempt by subtyping with the context; (b) keep it second. Taken: (b). The attempt with coercion cannot check a lambda argument (`checkApplicableWithCoercion` returns not applicable when an argument is unchecked, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:305`), so under (a) a call with a lambda argument whose instance only the expected type fixes would lose its only attempt that can accept it; and (b) does not pass over a fitting declaration for a coerced one, which is what the decision guards against, since its second attempt is still by subtyping. The fallback when no attempt is kept is unchanged in substance: the attempts with the context for a method invocation or operator, those without it for a call written `f(x)`.

**D5. Row 541's repair is in the constraint generation (`TypeAnalyzer.pSubInner`), not in the solver.** An argument of static type `L ∩ R` against a parameter type `$X` produced `pOr` of `L <: $X` and `R <: $X` (the intersection-on-the-left case comes before the inference-variable case), so the solver met a disjunction and took the branch that the set iteration put first: one conjunct, by declaration order, and on one program differently between two runs (row 541; the base run of this rung's tests shows the two messages, REPORT.md section 2). The solver cannot recover the intersection from the disjunction. One case placed before it makes an intersection a lower bound of an inference variable as a whole, the narrowest type the argument is substitutable for, which is the chapter's rule for one argument. It is the only edit of `TypeAnalyzer.scala`, outside `staticParam` (rung O's).

**D6. Row 535's pair becomes one compile test named `XXXInferLoneUnionClosedTrait.test`, and `InferLoneUnionClosedTraitLink.test` is removed.** The record says the link test is rewritten to `compile_err_contains` and the run test removed. The harness accepts a refusal only from an `XXX`-named `.test` file (`FileTests.java:932`, `shouldFail` from the file name; a plain file whose compile fails is a failure, `:384-404`), so the refusal is the `XXX` file, rewritten from `run` to `compile`, and the plain link file goes. The program writes `[\T extends Any\]`, so that the refusal names `BoxT[\Any\]`, the chapter's bound, and not the compile path's `Object` (row 412), as `InferLoneUnbounded` does.

**D7. The promoted pairs stay pairs.** Each run defect promoted (rows 447, 505, 508's three faces) keeps its plain link test and its run test, renamed without `XXX`, rather than one `.test` driving compile, link and run: one file fewer per pair would lower the compiler track's count (the gate's COUNT DOWN) for no gain. With the two new tests (`InferResultOnlyOverloaded`, `InferBigOperatorUnwritten`) and the split of `CoverageReturnInferred` (D8), the track's `.test` files go from 16 to 18 for these rows while one file is removed.

**Q1. Should rung O teach the checker the specification's Meet Rule for functional methods, so that the library gets no extra marker traits?**

- **A refresher.** A functional method is a method with `self` among its parameters that is called like a function, such as `x IN r`. The specification has two Meet Rules:
  - The rule for top-level functions asks, for any two overlapping declarations, for a third declaration on their meet.
  - The rule for functional methods asks that only of a type that provides both declarations.
- **What the checker does today.** It checks functional methods by the top-level rule too, so it is stricter than the specification's text. That is ledger row 556, gated by an expected failure.

Another 19 come from a separate capture defect that rung O fixes either way. The last 26 are true pairs inside one type, which rung M repairs either way.
- **Option a, the default.** Rung O teaches the checker the text's rule for functional methods. Rung M repairs only the 26. The library gains no markers the text does not ask for. If O's rule fails to land, the 78 wait one batch.
- **Option b.** Rung M adds about a dozen marker traits and headers to the library, as probe P2 measured on 09-28, to satisfy the checker's stricter check. Row 556 waits for a later checker rung. The markers stay in the library after the checker is fixed, true but not needed.
- **What a yes to a commits you to.** The checker follows the text's rule for functional methods. A family that mixes a top-level function with functional methods keeps today's check, because the text does not say which rule governs it; that is row 545. Walk is unchanged, and its missing rule stays row 544.
